intro_html: A home version inspired by the shop filling named above. The shops do not publish their recipes; these quantities are this site's own. This page makes one filling, then shapes and serves it. Start with plain cooked Japanese short-grain rice: rice cooking, hand shaping and all shop fillings →. The filling preparation time below excludes cooking the rice.

notes.html:
• Hidaka or quick-cooking kombu (hayani) is easier to soften for eating.
  • Thick dashi kombu can take longer.
  • If starting from dry kombu, hydrate it fully first, then weigh out 50 g.
  • The cooking time depends on the type and thickness.

• Do not reduce a chewy batch further.
  • Add enough water to cover and simmer gently again, checking a cooled strip until tender.
  • Recheck the seasoning afterwards.
  • This filling should stay moist; dried furikake is a different preparation.

• Fresh green shiso is green perilla, also sold as aojiso or oba: an aromatic, serrated green leaf.
  • Use fresh leaves here, not dried red shiso seasoning.
  • It adds fragrance, not softness; leaving it out does not change the kombu cooking method.
Keep the prepared filling, without rice, in the fridge for 4–5 days.

steps.body_html:
• Use 50 g drained, hydrated kombu left from dashi, not 50 g dry seaweed. Cut into strips about 2 mm wide and 3 cm long. Hydrated does not necessarily mean tender.
  • Put the kombu, 300 ml water and 1 tsp rice vinegar in a small pot. Bring to a boil, then simmer gently, partly covered. Keep the strips submerged: add water whenever the level drops. Do not add soy sauce, sugar or mirin yet.
  • Start checking after 20 minutes; thick kombu may need 60 minutes or longer. Cool a strip and bite it: it must cut through easily, without a leathery or stringy centre. Keep simmering with water until it passes this test; the clock is only a guide.
  • Reserve 50 ml cooking water, then drain. Return the tender kombu and reserved water to the pot; add the soy sauce, sugar and mirin. Simmer gently, stirring, about 10–15 minutes, until the sauce coats the strips and no loose puddle remains. Stop while the kombu is soft, moist and glossy; do not fry or dry it into furikake.
  • Turn off the heat and stir in the fresh green shiso (perilla), finely sliced. It is an aromatic Japanese herb; omit it if unavailable for a plain kombu filling. Let the filling cool before shaping.

how.caption: Slice hydrated dashi kombu into strips about 2 mm wide and 3 cm long; it still needs simmering until tender.
Only after the kombu passes the bite test, add the soy seasonings and reduce to a moist glaze. Add optional shiso off the heat.

steps.body_html:
• Have the cooked rice ready, covered, and cool it only until comfortable to hold. Wet your hands and rub a little salt over both palms.
  • For each onigiri, put about 60 g rice in your palm, make a well and add a heaped tablespoon of filling. Cover with another 60 g rice and gently close the rice around it. Save any extra filling separately.
  • Cup the rice from below with one hand. Bend the other hand into a roof, press gently to make a corner, turn a third of a turn and repeat. Keep it loose: press only enough to hold together.

how.caption: Glossy kombu and shiso in the well, enclosed with plain rice.

steps.body_html:
• For the shop-style finish, set a little of the same filling on top so you can see what is inside. Leave the top uncovered by nori.
  • Wrap one strip of nori around the base and up the sides just before serving. Eat within the hour while the nori is crisp. The sliced example shows the inside; cutting yours open is optional.
